en: The Thirteen-Book Collection of Birth Stories,
Chapter on Mangoes (Ambavagga)
10. The Sarabha Deer Birth Story:
“A wise person should indeed aspire; he should not become despondent.”
I see myself as I have become,
just as I desired. A person should indeed aspire thus.
The wise person should not despair;
for I see myself as one who has been pulled from the water onto dry land.
A wise person should indeed exert effort and not become despondent;
for I see myself [in this state].
Just as he wished, so it came to pass.
A wise person should indeed strive; he should not become despondent.
I see myself as one who has been pulled from the water onto dry land.
Even when beset by suffering, a man of wisdom—
One should not cut off hope for the arrival of happiness;
for many contacts, both harmful and beneficial,
approach a mortal while they are still unthought.
Even what is not thought of comes to pass,
and even what is thought of perishes;
for wealth is not produced by mere thinking.
“Whether for a woman or for a man.
“O Sarabha, that which you formerly followed in the mountain fastnesses;”
You live off one whose mind is not cowed,
who has rescued you from the difficult-to-cross hells.
Having fashioned a trap from stone,
the hawk brought him to suffering; yet he released him from the jaws of death,
and you spoke of that deer whose mind was undaunted.
“Were you yourself there at that time,
or did someone else tell this to you?
Are you one whose veil is removed, seeing all?”
“Is this knowledge, O Brahmin, of such a terrifying nature?
“I was not there at that time,
nor did anyone explain it to me.”
“O Lord of Men, the wise bring forth the meaning of well-spoken verses at such times.
“Taking up the shield that destroys the prowess of others,”
Why do you hesitate regarding the arrow on the bow?
Let the discharged arrow swiftly slay the deer;
for this, O one of supreme wisdom, is another [duty] of the king.
“Truly, I too understand this,
O Brahmin: that the deer honors the Kṣatriya for food provided in the past.”
"Therefore, O Great King, I shall not kill this deer.
"This is no deer, O Great King;
he is Asurasena, the Lord of Disā."
Having slain him, O lord of men,
become the sovereign of the immortals.
And if you, O King, should still have doubts, [then listen:]
"O best of heroes among men, you shall go to Vetaraṇī,
the river of Yama, along with your friends— the elephant, the deer, and the antelope— and together with your sons and wife."
“Granted, I and all the people of the countryside,
my sons, my wives, and my circle of friends—
let us all go together to that Vaitaraṇī River of Yama.”
But I would never kill one who gives me life.
This deer has been my benefactor when I was alone and in distress in this terrible, desolate forest.
Remembering such prior duties,
O Great Brahmā, how could I knowingly kill?
May you live long, delighting in your friends.
Rule this kingdom through the virtues of the Dhamma;
attended by throngs of women,
rejoice in the realm like Vāsava in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Free from anger, with a mind always serene,
having become one who offers hospitality to all guests and is devoted to giving,
he gives and eats according to his means.
"Blameless, you shall go to the heavenly realm.
The Sarabhamiga Jātaka, the tenth.
The Thirteenth Chapter is finished.
Its summary verse:
The excellent mango, the axe, the swan, the excellent one,
Then the wild one, the messenger, and the fifth.
Then there was Bodhi, Akitti, and Sutakka;
then Ruru and another, Sarabha.
